name: Phlox Pink
lede: Phlox Pink is a dusty lilac, the paler, lower-chroma member of the Phlox name family, and it differs from its vivid parent by losing almost all of the saturation.

sections.title: The pale cousin
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records this name on plate 41 E 4, with a first recorded date of 1912, six years earlier than [[phlox|Phlox]] itself [1]. The two names share the flower, but almost nothing else in color: [[phlox|Phlox]] is a near-saturated magenta, while Phlox Pink reads as the ISCC-NBS block "light purple", with low chroma and a soft, greyed cast [2]. Our library's own distance between the two Phlox names is 2.2 units — close, but not identical [2].

The nearest other named color is [[hay-s-lilac|Hay's Lilac]], 3.8 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[heather|Heather]] and [[dusty-lavender|Dusty Lavender]] close behind [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Phlox Pink appears in just 2 of our 23,781 paintings, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in only 1, rarer than 86 percent of our named colors [3]. Both matches come from the same painter, Paul Sérusier, between 1894 and 1898, and the color plays no large, prominent role in either canvas [3]. With a sample this thin, the finding describes two specific paintings, not a reliable pattern across his work [3].

By contrast, [[phlox|Phlox]] itself, the far more saturated parent name, has no match at all in the archive at the one-percent-of-canvas threshold, so neither Phlox name is well represented in museum collections as photographed [3]. That is consistent with both being late, commercial color names rather than traditional pigment words painters reached for before the twentieth century [3].
